analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from issuing any rule or assessment unless all underlying scientific data is publicly reproducible.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in June 2015 with a report carrying minority views from committee Democrats, was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a vote from the full Senate before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited the EPA from proposing, finalizing, or even publishing any risk assessment, standard, regulation, or guidance unless every piece of scientific and technical information behind it was the 'best available science,' specifically identified, and posted online in a way that allowed independent analysts to substantially reproduce the research. On its face that is a transparency requirement. In practice, it would have barred the agency from relying on long-term public health studies — such as landmark air-pollution epidemiology built on confidential patient records — that cannot be republished without violating patient privacy, making many major health-based rules legally impossible to issue. The bill also capped the EPA's cost of complying at $1 million per year.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by the EPA — power plants, refineries, chemical manufacturers, and other sources of air and water pollution — gain the most if the bill passes. A rule that cannot be justified with fully publishable data is far easier to challenge in court and far slower to issue, delaying or blocking pollution limits. Supporters also made a good-faith transparency argument: that the public has a right to verify the data behind regulations that cost it money.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require every EPA action — assessments, standards, limits, regulations, and even guidance — to rest on scientific information that is publicly available online in a manner sufficient for independent analysis and substantial reproduction [S2][S4].
Supporters' stated rationale is accountability: regulations with major costs should be verifiable by independent scientists rather than resting on data the public cannot see [S1].

The bill explicitly barred the EPA from using the requirement to censor scientific terms about climate change, pollution, or toxic exposure, and required the agency to implement it within a $1 million annual budget [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People who breathe polluted air or live near toxic sites pay if the bill passes. The EPA's most protective health rules — limits on fine particulate pollution, ozone, and toxic chemicals — rest in significant part on epidemiological studies whose underlying patient-level data is confidential by law. Under this bill those rules could not be proposed or finalized, so known health risks would go unregulated while the science behind them sat unusable.
analysis.who_pays_short: People exposed to air and toxic pollution

drawbacks.text: The data-availability requirement is absolute: no EPA proposal, final rule, or even guidance document could rely on any study whose raw data cannot be republished, which sweeps in confidential medical records protected by federal privacy law [S2][S4].

The bill lets a compliance-technique question — whether data is publishable — override the statutory mandate to use the 'best available science,' so a stronger study could be excluded in favor of a weaker but fully public one [S4].

The good-faith case for the bill is real: independent verification of government science is a legitimate demand, and some EPA-cited studies historically limited outside researchers' access to underlying data. A narrower version — protecting privacy while enabling controlled access — was the honest alternative supporters could have pursued.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency goal is legitimate, but the bill's design swapped a privacy problem for a prohibition. Rather than creating a controlled-access system so outside scientists could verify confidential health data, it simply made any rule resting on such data unissuable. The practical effect falls on the public in the form of delayed or unattainable pollution limits, while the litigation advantage flows to regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on a party-line basis, was placed on the Senate's calendar of general business in June 2015, and sat there without ever coming up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barrasso introduced the bill on February 24, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S6].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 28, 2015 [S6].

On June 22, 2015, Chairman Inhofe reported the bill with an amendment (Report No. 114-69), minority views were filed, and the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders [S3][S6].
No further action was taken; the bill never reached the Senate floor for a vote, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA and the public-health rules it issues came out ahead: the agency kept its existing ability to rely on the best available science, including confidential-data health studies, and no new procedural barrier to clean air and toxic-chemical rules was enacted. Industries seeking an easier path to challenge EPA rules gained nothing from the bill's death beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The EPA and existing pollution rules

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 24, 2015 and led its push in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Moved the bill through committee and formally reported it to the Senate with an amendment on June 22, 2015, placing it on the legislative calendar.

for.name: Seven Senate Republican cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (Vitter, Inhofe, Crapo, Fischer, Risch, Enzi, Flake)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans.

for.name: Regulated industries and their trade associations
for.role: Business groups opposing EPA air and toxics regulation
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill as a way to require publishable data behind EPA rules and open agency science to challenge.

against.name: Senate EPW Committee Democrats
against.role: Minority members, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Filed minority views against the committee report on June 22, 2015, opposing the bill as reported.

against.name: Scientific and public health organizations
against.role: Groups including the American Association for the Advancement of Science and major public health and medical associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the 'secret science' legislation, warning it would force the EPA to ignore the strongest long-term health studies because patient-level data is confidential.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican (8 senators total), the committee reported the bill with minority views filed by Democrats, and the bill advanced through committee without bipartisan support [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill would have made EPA health-based rules far harder to issue and easier to challenge, since rules resting on confidential-data epidemiology could not be proposed at all. The cost lands on people exposed to air and water pollution.

EPA risk, exposure, and hazard assessments — the backbone of toxic chemical limits — were covered actions under the bill, so assessments relying on non-publishable data would be barred. Weaker or slower assessments mean less restrictive chemical rules.

industries.industry: Environmental regulators and the public health research community
industries.note: The EPA would have lost the ability to rely on the best available science whenever it included confidential data, and researchers' confidential-data studies would become unusable for federal rulemaking. Their loss is directly the public's loss in health protection.
